title: The persecution of 845
hook: a Tang emperor closes the monasteries; the teachings that needed little come through

segments.voice: Yesterday: Baizhang, and a Chan monastery where work, meals and sitting made one life. Your line: work is practice.

Bells are being lowered from temple towers and carted off to be melted down. Bronze images follow them into the furnaces. Monks and nuns are told to take off their robes and go home as ordinary subjects. The gates are shut. This is China under the Tang emperor Wuzong, and a monk from Japan, far from home, is writing it all down in his diary while he tries to get himself and his books out of the country. When the buildings go, what's left?
screen: `BELLS GO TO THE FURNACE.` → `ROBES COME OFF.` → `WHAT'S LEFT?`

segments.voice: The official histories of the Tang dynasty date the harshest of Wuzong's decrees to 845. The court had come to see the monasteries as a drain: land, metal and people outside the tax rolls, serving a teaching from abroad. Wuzong himself favored Daoist masters. His decrees closed monasteries across the empire and sent monks and nuns back to lay life. The monk from Japan was Ennin, and his diary lets us see it from the road: monks forced into lay clothes, images stripped, foreign monks sent away. To get home, he put on ordinary clothes himself. The worst of it was short; the histories tell that Wuzong died soon after, and the next emperor eased the ban. But schools that leaned on great libraries, rich estates and the court's favor were badly shaken. A common way of telling the story is that two schools came through more easily. Chan, whose monks, like Baizhang's, worked their own fields and taught face to face. And Pure Land, whose practice could be carried in a single breath: the name of Amitabha Buddha, said by anyone, anywhere, with no building at all. Underneath is an old teaching of the Buddha: all conditioned things pass away. An empire can take bells, roofs and robes. It is much harder to confiscate a habit of sitting still, or a name a grandmother says over the stove. So a week that began with Bodhidharma facing a wall ends with stories saying the teaching did not live in the buildings.
screen: `AN EMPEROR'S DECREES.` · `ENNIN'S DIARY SAW IT.` · `WHAT NEEDED LITTLE CAME THROUGH.` · `ALL CONDITIONED THINGS PASS.` · then, large: `WHAT SURVIVED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that came through a hard time and reached you: a recipe in someone's handwriting, a song a parent sang, an old building on your street, a habit you kept through a bad year. Notice what it needed in order to last, and what it turned out not to need. If you'd like, bow to it slightly, with your head or only in your mind.
Ennin. The Japanese monk whose diary recorded the closing of China's monasteries under Emperor Wuzong, in 845.
Your line: what survived. Bells can be melted; a practice is harder to take. That's the week.

howItsDone: Chinese Buddhists remember the persecution under Emperor Wuzong as one of the hard turns in their history, and Chan and Pure Land communities often tell it as part of their own story of carrying the teaching through.

what a scholar hears: the Tang histories date it to 845, and Ennin, a monk from Japan, saw it on the road and wrote it in his diary.

chat.says: When China closed its monasteries in 845, did Buddhism there just end?
options: No. The worst was short, and practices needing little, like Chan and Pure Land, came through.
Yes. Once the buildings were gone, the teaching vanished from China for good.
No, because the emperor closed only the Chan halls and spared everyone else.
chat.meaning: The histories say Wuzong died soon after and the ban eased; a common telling says Chan and Pure Land, which traveled light, came through more easily.
